- https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/issues/4381

Several of these changes where already proposed earlier in separate PRs and/or might get split out. Here's a list:

review_comments: defer the allocation once needed?
If we get here, then it is needed because there are claims which need to be allocated.

Why the change to use `.t.Run`, to break this out by GVK?
Yes.

It failed for ResourceClaimList, but I couldn't do a `dlv test ...  -- -test.run=...` where I debugged just that one failure.
I have one more update for this: by creating the fuzzer anew for each sub-test, they become truly independent. The odd behavior from the commit message (failure when running all tests, passing when running just the sub-test) came from reusing the fuzzer because the randomness was different.
@bart0sh we are OK completely removing support for annotations? All runtimes have supported `ContainerConfig.CDIDevice` long enough, that we don't expect this to be a problem?
See https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/125210 - we agreed to make that change in 1.31.
Correct, we can do it now.
Is this all governed by gate "DRAControlPlaneController" now?
Yes. Fixed.

I found one use for a `class.status`: we could add a standard `conditions` field there with one standardized condition "faulty" (name TBD) which gets set when one of the CEL expressions causes a runtime error.

We could do the same for `claim.status` and `claimtemplate.status`.

None of that has a chance of being in 1.31, but as we might add it later, perhaps it makes sense to already add the `class.spec` indirection now?
I would *not* make the spec immutable. That breaks `kubectl apply -f driver-deployment.yaml` and any consumer of a class should be prepared for the class to get replaced *or* updated at any time.
Agreed, let's add spec now. It's not immutable, but it *is* only taken into account at scheduling / allocation time. So, if it is changed, we're not going to reschedule anything according to the new criteria.

I would probably use `Ready` as the `ConditionType`. Or maybe `Valid`.
Same as above, maybe I misunderstand what "stored" means?
See https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/125488#discussion_r1680478132

Should we be consistent in the naming of the types here? Why `DeviceRequest` and `DeviceConstraint`, but then `DeviceClaimConfiguration`? Should they all have `Claim` in the name (or not have it, for that matter)?
The `Claim` here is needed because the different `*Configuration` structs are slightly different.
I read the question as "why not DeviceClaimConstraint and DeviceClaimRequest".  IMO those would be more verbose for no real gain.  Claim config and class config are different, as Patrick said.
Do we not need to validate the status as well, or is that unnecessary since it is a subresource?
The status doesn't change during an update of the main resource and thus doesn't need to be validated. That's the common pattern.
Could we get away with DNS Label?

This is not user-facing and is in practice (= `resourceslicecontroller.go`) a generated name:
```
GenerateName: c.owner.Name + "-" + c.driver + "-",
```

That code will have to become a bit more careful about replacing slash with hyphen, otherwise the base name might not be a DNS label.

But that's doable, so yes. I'll simplify it.

Isn't the drive name a DNS subdomain though? How can we construct a DNS label out of
```
GenerateName: c.owner.Name + "-" + c.driver + "-",
```
if `c.driver` is a DNS subdomain?

That's what I meant with "replacing slash with hyphen" - oops, I meant "dot". Here's what the new code would have to look like:
```
GenerateName: strings.ReplaceAll(c.driver + "-" + c.owner.Name + "-", ".", "-"),
```

Note that this puts the driver name first because it's likely to be shorter. I remember some clusters have really long generated node names and that part is less important.

As I am making this change, I keep finding places where some other name is used as ResourceSlice name. For example, the unique namespace name is used also for a unique per-test ResourceSlice in one E2E test which simulates network-attached devices.

I'm not seeing any other usage of NameIsDNSLabel besides ValidateNamespaceName. Should we perhaps stick with the NameIsDNSSubdomain for consistency with pretty much all other API resources? Or am I missing some other cases?
I am fine with it, I just want to make sure we are not just copying patterns for no good reason.  Non-namespaces objects tend to want more unique names, and that is fine.

nit: s/uses/used/

Don't love the non-deterministic nature of this, seems likely to create flakes. But that pre-dates this change it seems. Does this particular instance take any materially larger amount of time?
No, it's a few seconds before and after. Each individual gvk doesn't take long, it just adds up.
It's reallyunclear to me what this test is achieveing.  AFAICT, all it does is prove that 1 field got a default value, 1 time.  It does not prove that it was CORRECT or that it got ALL of them, just that it changed one thing one time.  And as this PR shows it is non-deterministic.

Why not set this to 10K or 100K or 1M?

> It's really unclear to me what this test is achieveing. [...]

I think your analysis is correct. I suppose it was written because a generic validation test is still better than no test at all, but I am just guessing.

> Why not set this to 10K or 100K or 1M?

If it's too large, then a gvk with no defaulting might really run too long.
I am not sure it's better to wait in that case. But moot now anyway, we can discuss it when we add scoring.

Going back to the dicussion from https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/125488/files#r1669476527, is it not weird to call this `Controller` but call that `Driver`? They should either both be `Driver` or both be more specific, i.e. `Controller` and `Plugin`?
Replied in https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/125488#discussion_r1670170548.
You can resolve this
nitpicking, since I know the above topic is not resolved, but this says "device" - -- unless it is nested under a `device` header somewhere, shouldn't it be `resource`?
Will update as part of https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/125488#discussion_r1662958151.

This is the same struct as in the api.proto. I defined it again because I didn't want to make the checkpoint depend directly on an API definition that could change - that is what caused https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/123552.

We still need versioning to handle the situation that we need to extend the checkpoint content.

Perhaps this was decided long ago, but should we be using the word "plugin" instead? Granted, that could be confused with "device plugin", but "device driver" also has other meanings and may lead to confusion. I think people hear "driver" and think it's a kernel module or something, rather than  DRA kubelet plugin.

Perhaps it's just me, but I see "the kubelet plugin" of a DRA driver as only one of its pieces. Even without classic DRA and its control plane controller it might still have pieces for validation of configs (either configuration via VAP or some actual webhook).

As you said, "kubelet plugin" also isn't a good name.

I'd vote for using "Kubelet DRA plugin" as in my understanding it is a Kubelet plugin as it uses Kubelet plugin registration APIs also used by Device and CSI **plugins**. I agree with @johnbelamaric that "driver" sounds much more confusing.

We went back and forth on this many times in various objects when working on "classic" DRA. I know we had `KubeletPlugin` in one of the objects at one point and @thockin suggested we change it to `Driver`, so we did. I personally, don't feel too strongly about the name, but we need to pick one and commit to it.

CSI doesn't use the word "plugin". It uses "driver", just like DRA does:

https://kubernetes-csi.github.io/docs/drivers.html

So CSI is actually an argument **in favor** of keeping the "driver" terminology, not **against** it...

> it is a Kubelet plugin as it uses Kubelet plugin registration

That is an implementation detail that most users will not be aware of.

In https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/125488/files#discussion_r1670044997 @klueska pointed out that for the control plane controller we are more specific and call it "controller" because that is the function that gets referenced.

If this field here was part of the allocation result, then *maybe* I could be convinced to call the field "plugin" there in analogy to the "controller" field because that's another function of the driver.

But this here is not necessarily a kubelet plugin. If the driver is managing network-attached devices, then  "the DRA driver providing the capacity information" is not a kubelet plugin. Calling it "plugin" would be wrong, unless we interpret the word as "plugin for the cluster", which is just confusing.

Therefore I am against renaming this field here. When focusing only on structured parameters, we don't have the "controller" field. I therefore prefer to keep the structured parameters API consistent and use "driver" everywhere, with "controller" the only exception for classic DRA.
Makes sense to me, let's stick with driver.
If the selectors have not changed, can't we just skip validating them entirely?

I asked about that on Slack in the context of the immutable ResourceClaimSpec and ResourceClaimTemplateSpec: https://kubernetes.slack.com/archives/C0EG7JC6T/p1720529037793189

The recommendation there was to (re-)validate unchanged fields. I am not entirely convinced, but I am following that guidance.

For CEL validation, the tooling explicitly supports validating "stored" expressions. If they are "stored", they are by definition "unchanged" and thus shouldn't need to be validated again. So perhaps there are reasons to validate again that I just don't understand.
See also https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/125488#discussion_r1680599181

Do we need to allow subdomain (253 with dots) or can we get away with DNS label (63, no dots)?

No strong opinion.

@klueska ?

I have historically been using `gpu.nvidia.com` as the "default" class name (to mimic the default extended resource name of `nvidia.com/gpu`). Can I flip the question around -- is there a strong reason *not* to allow a subdomain?

Allowing domains might indeed be useful, not just to mimic traditional behavior but also to avoid name clashes between classes defined by different vendors. We don't have any guidelines for classes, but if we had, then "name ends with a domain owned by the vendor" would make sense for classes that come straight from a vendor.

This is more of a less-is-more question.  There's a whole lot of cargo-culting in validation, and using domains rather than labels has occasionally caused problems.  As long as we are doing it for a reason, I am OK with it.  For non-namespaces objects it seems less likely to be a problem than namespaced things.

+required?  

Comment: is this allowed to go backwards?  is this allowed to increment by arbitrary jumps?

> +required

Added.

> is this allowed to go backwards?

Not if there are existing slices. If all of them are deleted, then I think it's okay to start again at 0. There's a slight race where a scheduler might still use the "old" pool that already got deleted while a driver which right at that moment starts up, sees no slices, and starts publishing with `generation: 0`, but I think that's part of the unavoidable "scheduler might use out-dated information" problem.

The generation serves as signal for "pool is being updated", not for "pool information is the latest". We can indicate the former, but not the latter.

Added a paragraph about this.

>  is this allowed to increment by arbitrary jumps?

Yes. s/increment/increase/?

I just want the comments here to be robust enough to implement against.  Given int64, I doubt we have to worry about rollover (even with JSON dropping it to 56 bits or something like that).

So, is this really implementable?  As a driver author, does this mean I need to track a pool's state somewhere?  Consider a long-lived node.  Upgrades of that node might involve totally nuking the OS and drivers and bringing it up from scratch.  If that is allowed, how does the new driver set generation?  Does it have to RMW all of the slices?  Or does it store a CR with per-driver, per-node state?

What will be the implementation guidance here?

I'm  probably not wording it well :cry: 

Resetting to zero is okay, so drivers don't need to remember any previous state. If they know about some existing slices, they should use a higher generation in their next update because it provides some early indication to the consumer that newer slices are coming while the older slices are being deleted.

This goes back to a problem with the assume cache (pre-dates this PR): if a user of an assume cache modifies an item, then stores that modified item in the cache *before* sending the update to the apiserver, then any update of that item coming from the apiserver is seen as "newer" and the local modification gets lost.

We must not loose the "allocated" state, but neither do we want to do blocking API calls here. The solution is tracking of "in flight claims": those have the local modification which will get applied to the apiserver later.

Triggered by the "why re-validate unchanged fields" question I am starting to wonder about the common (right?) practice of calling the normal validate function for create as part of an update, like I am doing here.

`spec.Config` contains a one-of. We check that `Opaque` is set. Suppose the following:
- In 1.32, we add an alternative.
- Someone creates a DeviceClass with a config using that alternative.
- They downgrade to 1.31.
- The DeviceClass is now invalid (empty one-of).

What operations should be allowed in that state?

An update which removes the config works, the updated DeviceClass is valid again.

Reading the DeviceClass works. Clients bulk at processing it because they check the one-of. Also okay.

What about deleting the DeviceClass? I suppose if it can be removed directly, it's okay. But if it has a finalizer, the DeviceClass must be updated (add DeletionTimestamp), which probably fails.

Thinking this through further, this might be the reason why "unchanged" fields should be re-validated: if the current apiserver does not support some future field, then any update will drop that field because the apiserver doesn't know how to re-encode it. Validation is not guaranteed to catch this, but it does for one-ofs and enums. So if an "apparently" unmodified field no longer passes validation, it's likely that the apiserver lacks something and it might be better to not update the resource because that would drop information.

You left out feature gates.

* `spec.Config` contains a one-of. We check that `Opaque` is set.
* In 1.32 we move DRA to beta (on by default)
* In 1.32, we add an alternative config under a new gate, which is alpha
* Someone enables that alpha gate and creates a DeviceClass with a config using that alternative.
* They downgrade to 1.31.
* The DeviceClass is now invalid (empty one-of).

There's no rollback-safety when using alpha gates.  If instead:

* `spec.Config` contains a one-of. We check that `Opaque` is set.
* In 1.32 we move DRA to beta (on by default)
* In 1.32, we add an alternative config under a new gate, which is alpha
* In 1.33 we move that new gate to beta
* Someone creates a DeviceClass with a config using that alternative.
* They downgrade to 1.32.
* The DeviceClass is now valid because of the "already in use" logic

We COULD say that one-ofs are allowed to have no value set, and consumers should ignore them, but we usually don't because it makes edge-cases that don't need to exist.
